extracted.intended_audience: writers, screenwriters, comic/webcomic creators, television/radio producers, and general readers interested in narrative structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for constructing and understanding story arcs (narrative arcs) across media such as novels, television, comics, webcomics, film, manga, and radio. Covers purpose, common structures (three-act, hero's journey), serialization issues, and format-specific practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a story arc / narrative arc
rubrics_metrics.description: A story arc (also narrative arc) is the chronological construction of a plot in a novel or story; it can also mean an extended or continuing storyline in episodic storytelling media such as television, comic books, comic strips, board games, video games, and films with each episode following a dramatic arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists the media in which story arcs appear and notes that in different media arcs may span many episodes; mentions that in a traditional Hollywood film the story arc usually follows a three-act structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of a story arc: effect change
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of a story arc is to move a character or a situation from one state to another, in other words, to effect change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change often takes the form of either a tragic fall from grace or a reversal from weakness to strength (examples: a poor woman makes a fortune; a lonely man falls in love and marries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero's journey / monomyth as a form of arc
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'hero's journey' (Joseph Campbell's monomyth) is another form of storytelling that offers a change or transformation of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christopher Vogler's The Writer's Journey adapts the monomyth specifically for western storytelling; cited as a commonly used arc template by writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act structure in traditional Hollywood film
rubrics_metrics.description: In a traditional Hollywood film, the story arc usually follows a three-act structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three-act structure is presented as the common dramatic organization for films, linking story arcs to established dramatic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of arcs in television and radio (multi-episode arcs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story arcs on television and radio have existed for decades and are common where multi-episode storylines are the norm; on a television program the story may unfold over many episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arc-based series can be short-lived and difficult to attract new viewers or syndicate, but DVD box sets and streaming help by giving easy access to relevant episodes; soap operas are an area where arcs have always thrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arcs draw and reward dedicated viewers; fan practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Arc-based series draw and reward dedicated viewers; fans follow and discuss different story arcs independently from particular episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arcs are sometimes split into subarcs significant to fans; episodes not relevant to arcs ('villain of the week') may be dismissed as filler by fans but might be called stand-alone by producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Webcomics and archives encourage arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: Webcomics are more likely to use story arcs than newspaper comics, as most webcomics have readable archives online that a newcomer to the strip can read in order to understand what is going on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short story arcs are easier to package as trade paperbacks for resale and are more accessible to casual readers than never-ending continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic-book issue arc lengths and packaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Many American comic book series are now written in four- or six-issue arcs, within a continuing series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short arcs facilitate packaging as trade paperbacks and resale, making them more accessible than long-running continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity absence prevents permanent change / no growth
rubrics_metrics.description: A corollary to the absence of continuity is that no permanent change to characters or situations occurs, meaning no growth can take place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 1950s DC Superman comics where lack of continuity led to repeating storylines; implies that continuity supports lasting character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arc structure and length in manga and anime
rubrics_metrics.description: Manga and anime are usually good examples of arc-based stories; most series shorter than twenty-six chapters are a single arc spanning all the chapters, while series of thirty chapters or longer usually have multiple arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This serial structure makes syndication difficult because episodes watched in isolation often confuse viewers; examples cited include Neon Genesis Evangelion (single 26-episode arc) and long-running series like One Piece and Naruto having multiple arcs.
